name: Arawá
confidence_why: Arawá is extinct and its whole record is Chandless's 1869 list of 52 words, where a Portuguese-style acute sits on the last syllable of 50 words and might mark stress but is never explained as a rule (the convention he borrowed from Martius 1863 also marks vowel quality and hiatus), while Dixon 1999 and Dienst 2008 say nothing about stress, so any reading such as final stress is an inference from diacritics rather than a description.
catalog_citation: Chandless, William. 1869. Notes of a Journey up the River Juruá. Journal of the Royal Geographical Society 39: 296-311.
catalog_locator: p. 311 (;ernet.dli.2015.70705), 'Arauá Words' table (52 entries) and the orthographic note beneath it; read on p. 311 at 200 and, because the archive.org drops accents
catalog_quote: ARAUÁ WORDS. [column heads: English. / Arauá.] Turtle: Chirifuá. Male turtle (capitary): Camará. Tracajá: Chirí. Male tracajá: Jujú. Peixe-boi (sea-cow): Afina. Tapir: Awí. Dog: Jumayhí (English j). Tortoise: Coasá. Fish: Abaigauá. Wild Pig: Isama. Taititú: Nubasá. Mutum (curassow-bird): Fazú. Mutum-assu: Arí-borí. Hen: Tacará. Eggs: Nafariná. Banana: Fanará. Tobacco (or "parica"): Agá. Calabash: Wáú. India-rubber: Carú. Copaiba oil: Awá-tinaní. Bark-canoe: Awa-safiný. Lake: Dacú-fuá. Yuca: Fou ou-maunidí. House: Zamí. Axe: Barí. Sun: Mahí. Moon: Massicú. Water (and river): Pahá. Fire: Si-hú. Star: Amóa-huá. One: Warihí. Two: Famihí. Three: Arisafahá. Yes: Naida-á. No: Hina-á. Good: Amozadí. Bad: Amozaraha-dí. Sick: Amozarahá-nahadí. Plenty: Toodí. A lie: Timaudí. Man: Maquidá. Woman: Waidauá. Boy: Ganahí-quidauá. Father: Abí. Mother: Amí. Hand: Usafá. Foot: Otamá. Bow: Bigauahá. Arrow: Atú. Oar: Waramí. Knife: Zui-mazarú. Cutlass (terçado): Sara-sará. [Note beneath the table:] The spelling (or the pronunciation) is as in Portuguese; this having been adopted in the 'Glossaria Linguarum Brasiliensum;' excepting that w has been used, where wanted; and h is an aspirate. The Arauá language is pronounced with tolerable distinctness, except with respect to f and h, which it is very difficult in some cases to distinguish. Manáos, January 21st, 1869.

The Arauá language is pronounced with tolerable distinctness, except with respect to f an…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chandless never states a rule. But his 52-item list carries an acute accent on the last syllable of 50 of the 52 words, and he says the spelling/pronunciation follows Portuguese as in Martius's Glossaria, where the acute marks the tonic syllable (Martius 1863: 29, 'die Sylbe zu betonen'). Read at face value, Arawá word stress fell on the final syllable, and each element of a compound carried its own final accent (Arí-borí 'mutum-assu', Awá-tinaní 'copaiba oil', Amozarahá-nahadí 'sick', Ganahí-quidauá 'boy').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Compounds show an accent on each element (e.g. Arí-borí, Awá-tinaní, Dacú-fuá, Zui-mazarú), which could be read as one stress per element.
new_statements.exceptions: Two words written without any accent: Afina 'peixe-boi (sea-cow)', Isama 'wild pig' (under the Portuguese convention an unaccented word in -a would be penult-stressed). One non-final accent: Amóa-huá 'star' (accent on the first element's penult plus the final). Chandless notes only that f and h were hard to distinguish.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in an explorer's 52-word list collected in 1867 on the Juruá; no sentences, no morphology. The stress reading is an inference from diacritics under the transcriber's declared convention, not a linguist's statement; Dixon 1999: 293 calls the list 'rather well transcribed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog arua1263 = the Arawá/Arauá of the Juruá after which the Arawan family is named (Chandless's 'Arauá', collected 1867 on the Juruá; tribe destroyed by measles soon after, Dixon 1999: 293). Do not confuse with Aruá (Tupian, Rondônia) or with Arawak. The 52-word list is the entire attestation; the stress reading applies to the variety Chandless heard at that one village.

sources.note: No stress rule is stated. The 52-word list writes an acute accent on the LAST syllable of 50 of 52 words (Chirifuá, Camará, Massicú, Pahá, Si-hú, Warihí, Famihí, Arisafahá, Maquidá, Waidauá, Zamí, Atú.; each element of a compound accented: Arí-borí, Awá-tinaní, Amozarahá-nahadí); unaccented: Afina, Isama; one non-final accent: Amóa-huá. Note on p. 311: spelling '(or the pronunciation) is as in Portuguese; this having been adopted in the Glossaria Linguarum Brasiliensum' - i.e. the acute marks the tonic syllable.

sources.citation: Dienst, Stefan. 2008 [online 2010]. The internal classification of the Arawan languages. LIAMES 8: 61-67. DOI 10.20396/liames.v8i1.1471.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Confirms Arawá 'is only known from a short wordlist collected by William Chandless in 1867' (52 items); reproduces Chandless's accented forms (awa-safiný 'bark-canoe', <si-hú> 'fire'); cites Dixon 2004a pp. 3, 38-39, 49, 58 for the Arawá cognates and Chandless 1869:311 on f/h.

sources.note: Nothing on Arawá stress. p. 293: 'For Arawá, after which the family is named, all we have is about fifty words taken down by the English explorer Chandless in 1867 (these are rather well transcribed); the tribe was wiped out shortly afterwards by an epidemic of measles.' Phonology section is Proto-Arawá segments; only stress mention is Sorowahá [ɨ] 'in unstressed position'.

sources.citation: Martius, C. F. P. von. 1863. Glossaria linguarum Brasiliensium / Wörtersammlung brasilianischer Sprachen. Erlangen: Junge. Einleitung p. 29 (orthographic conventions).
sources.note: Supporting only (the convention Chandless says he adopted): the acute accent (') 'dient, den Vocal zu schärfen oder die Sylbe zu betonen' - serves to sharpen the vowel or to stress the syllable. Contains no Arawá data.
